claim: Roughly half of all enzymes make use of metal centers to expand their chemical repertoire.
source: Roughly half of all enzymes make use of metal centers to expand their chemical repertoire (Waldron et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Waldron et al., 2009

claim: Fe-S clusters are thought to be the most ancient biological cofactors.
source: Among the most fascinating of the metallocofactors used for such purposes are Fe-S clusters, which are thought to be the most ancient biological cofactors and which enable chemical transformations ranging from simple electron transfer events to the formation and cleavage of carbon-carbon bonds (Rees and Howard, 2003; Beinert et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rees and Howard, 2003 and Beinert et al., 1997

claim: Fe-S clusters enable chemical transformations ranging from simple electron transfer events to the formation and cleavage of carbon-carbon bonds.
source: Among the most fascinating of the metallocofactors used for such purposes are Fe-S clusters, which are thought to be the most ancient biological cofactors and which enable chemical transformations ranging from simple electron transfer events to the formation and cleavage of carbon-carbon bonds (Rees and Howard, 2003; Beinert et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rees and Howard, 2003 and Beinert et al., 1997

claim: Complex Fe-S clusters catalyze fundamental redox conversions that are thought to have enabled early life on Earth.
source: Complex Fe-S clusters, containing alternative metal ions and/or expanded metal frameworks, such as the FeMo-cofactor of nitrogenase, the H-cluster of Fe-Fe hydrogenase, and the C-cluster of Ni-dependent carbon monoxide dehydrogenase (CODH), catalyze fundamental redox conversions that are thought to have enabled early life on Earth (Rees and Howard, 2003; Rees, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rees and Howard, 2003 and Rees, 2002

claim: Complex Fe-S clusters have been termed the 'great clusters' of biology.
source: Given their structural complexity and the essential nature of the reactions they catalyze, these clusters have collectively been termed the 'great clusters' of biology (Rees, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rees, 2002

claim: CODH catalyzes the interconversion of the gaseous pollutant CO and the greenhouse gas CO2.
source: In particular, CODH catalyzes the interconversion of the gaseous pollutant CO and the greenhouse gas CO2, leading to the removal of an estimated 108 tons of CO from the lower atmosphere each year and making it an attractive remediation tool (Bartholomew and Alexander, 1979).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bartholomew and Alexander, 1979

claim: CODH leads to the removal of an estimated 108 tons of CO from the lower atmosphere each year.
source: In particular, CODH catalyzes the interconversion of the gaseous pollutant CO and the greenhouse gas CO2, leading to the removal of an estimated 108 tons of CO from the lower atmosphere each year and making it an attractive remediation tool (Bartholomew and Alexander, 1979).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bartholomew and Alexander, 1979

claim: The anaerobic, Ni-dependent CODH has a homodimeric structure containing a total of five metalloclusters, called the B-, C-, and D-clusters.
source: The anaerobic, Ni-dependent CODH has a homodimeric structure containing a total of five metalloclusters, called the B-, C-, and D-clusters.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text

claim: The C-cluster is the site of CO/CO2 interconversion.
source: The C-cluster is the site of CO/CO2 interconversion and is composed of a [Ni-3Fe-4S] cubane connected through a linking sulfide (SL) to a unique iron site (Feu) (Figure 1) (Drennan et al., 2001; Dobbek et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Drennan et al., 2001 and Dobbek et al., 2001

claim: The C-cluster is composed of a [Ni-3Fe-4S] cubane connected through a linking sulfide (SL) to a unique iron site (Feu).
source: The C-cluster is the site of CO/CO2 interconversion and is composed of a [Ni-3Fe-4S] cubane connected through a linking sulfide (SL) to a unique iron site (Feu) (Figure 1) (Drennan et al., 2001; Dobbek et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Drennan et al., 2001 and Dobbek et al., 2001, and shown in Figure 1

claim: The C-cluster takes on four discrete redox states termed Cox, Cred1, Cint, and Cred2.
source: These studies have revealed the C-cluster to take on four discrete redox states termed Cox, Cred1, Cint, and Cred2 (Lindahl et al., 1990; Kumar et al., 1993; Anderson and Lindahl, 1994; Anderson and Lindahl, 1996; Seravalli et al., 1997; Fraser and Lindahl, 1999).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The most widely accepted mechanism of CO oxidation involves a one-electron reductive activation of the inactive Cox state to Cred1 followed by a catalytic cycle involving conversion between Cred1 and Cred2.
source: The most widely accepted mechanism of CO oxidation involves a one-electron reductive activation of the inactive Cox state to Cred1 followed by a catalytic cycle involving conversion between Cred1 and Cred2 (Figure 2) (Lindahl et al., 1990; Kim et al., 2004; Lindahl, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 2

claim: The overall fold and cluster placement of DvCODH is highly similar to other structurally characterized CODHs.
source: The overall fold and cluster placement of DvCODH is highly similar to other structurally characterized CODHs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Drennan et al., 2001; Dobbek et al., 2001; Domnik et al., 2017; Doukov et al., 2002; Darnault et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: DvCODH has a [2Fe-2S] cluster at the D-cluster position instead of the expected [4Fe-4S] cluster.
source: One noteworthy difference with respect to other CODHs is the identity of the D-cluster, a solvent-exposed Fe-S cluster at the dimer interface that serves as an electron conduit to the surface of the protein. Instead of the expected [4Fe-4S] cluster, (Drennan et al., 2001; Dobbek et al., 2001; Domnik et al., 2017; Doukov et al., 2002; Darnault et al., 2003) the electron density is consistent with a [2Fe-2S] cluster (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) as is the placement of cysteine residues in the primary structure.
evidence: Supported by electron density data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and sequence analysis

claim: DvCODH has a C-X2-C D-cluster binding motif instead of a C-X7-C motif.
source: CODH sequence alignments reveal that instead of a C-X7-C D-cluster binding motif, DvCODH, as well as several uncharacterized CODHs, have a C-X2-C motif (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The shortened C-X2-C motif constrains the geometry of the ligating cysteine residues such that coordination to a [4Fe-4S] cluster is not possible.
source: This shortened C-X2-C motif appears to constrain the geometry of the ligating cysteine residues such that coordination to a [4Fe-4S] cluster is not possible.
evidence: Inference based on structural analysis

claim: The cysteine positions in DvCODH are ideally suited for coordination of a [2Fe-2S] cluster.
source: Instead, the cysteine positions are ideally suited for coordination of a [2Fe-2S] cluster.
evidence: Inference based on structural analysis

claim: Two structures of as-isolated DvCODH using two independent protein batches display different conformations of the C-cluster.
source: In the present work, we determined two structures of as-isolated DvCODH using two independent protein batches and much to our surprise, we observe different conformations of the C-cluster in each structure.
evidence: Direct observation from crystallographic data

claim: A 2.50 Å resolution structure of as-isolated DvCODH (protein batch 1) displays the canonical [Ni-3Fe-4S]-Feu C-cluster.
source: A 2.50 Å resolution structure of as-isolated DvCODH (determined using protein batch 1) displays the canonical [Ni-3Fe-4S]-Feu C-cluster (Figure 3a; Figure 3—figure supplement 1a; Supplementary file 1) (Drennan et al., 2001; Gong et al., 2008; Doukov et al., 2002; Darnault et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a

claim: The ligation of the C-cluster is conserved in DvCODH with four cysteines ligating the cubane portion of the cluster.
source: The ligation of the C-cluster is conserved in DvCODH (Drennan et al., 2001; Dobbek et al., 2001; Gong et al., 2008; Domnik et al., 2017; Doukov et al., 2002; Darnault et al., 2003) with four cysteines ligating the cubane portion of the cluster (Cys519 is the Ni ligand); one histidine (His266) and one cysteine (Cys302) ligate Feu (Figure 3a; Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by citations and crystallographic data shown in Figure 3a

claim: Cys519 is the Ni ligand in the canonical C-cluster.
source: The ligation of the C-cluster is conserved in DvCODH (Drennan et al., 2001; Dobbek et al., 2001; Gong et al., 2008; Domnik et al., 2017; Doukov et al., 2002; Darnault et al., 2003) with four cysteines ligating the cubane portion of the cluster (Cys519 is the Ni ligand); one histidine (His266) and one cysteine (Cys302) ligate Feu (Figure 3a; Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3a

claim: His266 and Cys302 ligate Feu in the canonical C-cluster.
source: The ligation of the C-cluster is conserved in DvCODH (Drennan et al., 2001; Dobbek et al., 2001; Gong et al., 2008; Domnik et al., 2017; Doukov et al., 2002; Darnault et al., 2003) with four cysteines ligating the cubane portion of the cluster (Cys519 is the Ni ligand); one histidine (His266) and one cysteine (Cys302) ligate Feu (Figure 3a; Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3a

claim: The 1.72 Å structure of as-isolated DvCODH (protein batch 2) reveals a novel arrangement of ions within the C-cluster.
source: The second, higher-resolution (1.72 Å) structure of as-isolated DvCODH (determined using protein batch 2) reveals a novel arrangement of ions within the C-cluster that was confirmed using anomalous diffraction data (Figure 3b; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3b

claim: In the novel C-cluster arrangement, Ni, Feu, and SL are shifted, accompanied by conformational changes of several amino acid side chains, while the positions of the remaining three Fe and three S ions are unchanged.
source: In this structure, Ni, Feu, and SL are shifted, accompanied by conformational changes of several amino acid side chains, while the positions of the remaining three Fe and three S ions are unchanged.
evidence: Direct observation from crystallographic data

claim: In the novel C-cluster arrangement, the Ni ion is bound in the site formerly occupied by Feu, coordinated by His266 and Cys302.
source: The Ni ion is bound in the site formerly occupied by Feu, coordinated by His266 and Cys302 (Figure 3b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3b

claim: In the novel C-cluster arrangement, the Ni is additionally ligated by Cys519 and Lys556.
source: The Ni is additionally ligated by Cys519 and Lys556 (Figure 3b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3b

claim: Cys519 adopts an alternative rotamer conformation in the novel C-cluster arrangement such that coordination to Ni is maintained.
source: As mentioned above, Cys519 serves as a ligand to Ni in the canonical C-cluster and here adopts an alternative rotamer conformation such that coordination to Ni is maintained (Figure 3b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3b

claim: The occupancy of the alternative Cys519 conformation correlates with the occupancy of Ni, and both have been refined at an atomic occupancy of 70%.
source: The occupancy of the alternative Cys519 conformation correlates with the occupancy of Ni, and both have been refined at an atomic occupancy of 70%, in general agreement with the metal analysis result of 0.5 Ni per monomer for the sample that was crystallized (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic refinement and metal analysis data

claim: Metal analysis shows 0.5 Ni per monomer for the sample that was crystallized (protein batch 2).
source: The occupancy of the alternative Cys519 conformation correlates with the occupancy of Ni, and both have been refined at an atomic occupancy of 70%, in general agreement with the metal analysis result of 0.5 Ni per monomer for the sample that was crystallized (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by ICP-OES metal analysis data

claim: Lys556 is highly conserved and is the proposed general base catalyst for deprotonation of water during CO oxidation.
source: Lys556 is highly conserved and does not normally coordinate to the C-cluster, but is instead the proposed general base catalyst for deprotonation of water during CO oxidation (Figure 2) (Drennan et al., 2001; Dobbek et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Drennan et al., 2001, Dobbek et al., 2001, and Kim et al., 2004

claim: In the novel C-cluster arrangement, the lysine amine group comes within 2.5 Å of Ni.
source: Here, the lysine amine group comes within 2.5 Å of Ni.
evidence: Direct measurement from crystallographic data

claim: His266, Cys302, Cys519, and Lys556 ligate the Ni in the altered cluster in a highly distorted tetrahedral coordination geometry.
source: Together, His266, Cys302, Cys519, and Lys556 ligate the Ni in this altered cluster in a highly distorted tetrahedral coordination geometry that is reminiscent of the geometry of the Ni site in Ni-Fe hydrogenases (Volbeda et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data and comparison to Ni-Fe hydrogenases

claim: The Ni coordination geometry in the altered C-cluster is reminiscent of the geometry of the Ni site in Ni-Fe hydrogenases.
source: Together, His266, Cys302, Cys519, and Lys556 ligate the Ni in this altered cluster in a highly distorted tetrahedral coordination geometry that is reminiscent of the geometry of the Ni site in Ni-Fe hydrogenases (Volbeda et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Volbeda et al., 1995

claim: In the novel C-cluster arrangement, Feu is coordinated by Cys302, which forms a bridging interaction with Ni, and by Cys301.
source: In addition to interaction with SL, Feu is coordinated by Cys302, which forms a bridging interaction with Ni, and by a conserved cysteine residue (Cys301) that does not normally serve as a ligand to the C-cluster, resulting in an apparent three-coordinate geometry around Feu (Figure 3b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3b

claim: Cys301 is a conserved cysteine residue that does not normally serve as a ligand to the C-cluster.
source: In addition to interaction with SL, Feu is coordinated by Cys302, which forms a bridging interaction with Ni, and by a conserved cysteine residue (Cys301) that does not normally serve as a ligand to the C-cluster, resulting in an apparent three-coordinate geometry around Feu (Figure 3b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Direct statement based on structural comparison

claim: The shift in the positions of Feu and SL results in the loss of an interaction between SL and Fe1.
source: The shift in the positions of Feu and SL results in the loss of an interaction between SL and a second Fe ion of the cubane (Fe1), leaving Fe1 with three coordinating ligands, Cys340 and two cubane sulfides.
evidence: Direct observation from crystallographic data

claim: Fe1 has three coordinating ligands in the novel C-cluster arrangement: Cys340 and two cubane sulfides.
source: The shift in the positions of Feu and SL results in the loss of an interaction between SL and a second Fe ion of the cubane (Fe1), leaving Fe1 with three coordinating ligands, Cys340 and two cubane sulfides.
evidence: Direct observation from crystallographic data

claim: A small peak of residual electron density at a site bridging Feu and Fe1 is present in one of the protein chains in the asymmetric unit.
source: A small peak of residual electron density at a site bridging Feu and Fe1 is present in one of the protein chains in the asymmetric unit (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by electron density data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: The occupancy of the residual electron density site bridging Feu and Fe1 is low (<30%), precluding identification of the atom/ion.
source: The occupancy of this site is low (<30%) precluding identification of the atom/ion.
evidence: Direct statement based on crystallographic analysis

claim: If fully occupied, the atom/ion at the residual density site would complete the tetrahedral geometry around Feu and Fe1.
source: However, if fully occupied, the atom/ion would complete the tetrahedral geometry around these Fe atoms.
evidence: Inference based on structural analysis

claim: The two cubane S ions that coordinate Ni in the canonical cluster are left in a possibly unstable state in the altered conformation in which they could be susceptible to protonation or loss as free sulfide ions.
source: In addition to changes in Fe coordination, the altered conformation of the C-cluster also involves changes in sulfide coordination state. In particular, the two cubane S ions that coordinate Ni in the canonical cluster are left in a possibly unstable state in which they could be susceptible to protonation or loss as free sulfide ions (Crack et al., 2006).
evidence: Inference based on structural analysis and citation to Crack et al., 2006

claim: There is no evidence of degradation at the cubane sulfide sites in the altered C-cluster structure.
source: In our structure, however, we see no evidence of degradation at these sites, likely due to inaccessibility to solvent or other protective features of the protein environment, in analogy to the case of stable [3Fe-4S] clusters.
evidence: Direct observation from crystallographic data

claim: The lack of degradation at the cubane sulfide sites is likely due to inaccessibility to solvent or other protective features of the protein environment.
source: In our structure, however, we see no evidence of degradation at these sites, likely due to inaccessibility to solvent or other protective features of the protein environment, in analogy to the case of stable [3Fe-4S] clusters.
evidence: Inference based on structural analysis and comparison to stable [3Fe-4S] clusters

claim: Pre-formed crystals of as-isolated DvCODH (batch 2) incubated with sodium dithionite display the canonical C-cluster with Ni, Feu, and SL rearranged into their catalytically-relevant positions.
source: Pre-formed crystals of as-isolated DvCODH (batch 2, containing the altered cluster) were incubated with the reductant sodium dithionite. Strikingly, the resulting crystal structure displays the canonical C-cluster with Ni, Feu, and SL rearranged into their catalytically-relevant positions (Figure 4a,b; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 4a,b

claim: Oxidation of the reduced C-cluster by exposure to O2 results in reformation of the unusual cluster architecture.
source: To examine whether this metal rearrangement is reversible upon oxidation, crystals of reduced DvCODH were taken from the anaerobic chamber and incubated under ambient atmospheric conditions. Remarkably, oxidation of the reduced C-cluster by exposure to O2 results in reformation of the unusual cluster architecture (Figure 4c; Supplementary file 1)
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 4c

claim: Both the D- and B-clusters remain intact upon oxidation of the C-cluster by exposure to O2.
source: Remarkably, oxidation of the reduced C-cluster by exposure to O2 results in reformation of the unusual cluster architecture (Figure 4c; Supplementary file 1), whereas both the D- and B-clusters remain intact (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The altered cluster is an oxidized form of the C-cluster and the multi-metal ion rearrangement is reversible.
source: Together, these results suggest that this altered cluster is an oxidized form of the C-cluster and that this multi-metal ion rearrangement is reversible (Figure 4d, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: Inference based on crystallographic data showing reversible structural changes upon reduction and oxidation

claim: An EPR spectrum of dithionite-reduced DvCODH exhibits resonances characteristic of the one-electron reduced B- and D-clusters and of the Cred1 and Cred2 forms of the C-cluster.
source: First, an EPR spectrum was recorded on a sample of dithionite-reduced DvCODH. This spectrum exhibits resonances characteristic of the one-electron reduced B- and D-clusters (centered around g ~ 2) and of the Cred1 and Cred2 forms of the C-cluster (gav ~ 1.83 and 1.87, respectively; see Figure 2), as has been previously observed for DvCODH (Hadj-Saïd et al., 2015) (Figure 4e, black trace).
evidence: Supported by EPR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4e and citation to Hadj-Saïd et al., 2015

claim: A dithionite-reduced DvCODH sample incubated under ambient atmospheric conditions and then re-reduced with dithionite shows full recovery of the previously observed EPR signals.
source: A parallel dithionite-reduced sample was incubated under ambient atmospheric conditions to mimic treatment of the DvCODH crystals (EPR-silent, data not shown). The oxygen-exposed sample was then re-reduced with dithionite and the EPR spectrum was recorded, revealing full recovery of the previously observed signals (Figure 4e, red trace).
evidence: Supported by EPR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4e

claim: The metalloclusters of DvCODH are not degraded upon oxidation.
source: Combined, our crystal structures and EPR data reveal that the metalloclusters of DvCODH are not degraded upon oxidation and that the C-cluster avoids degradation by adopting an alternative, stable, oxidized conformation.
evidence: Inference based on combined crystallographic and EPR data

claim: The C-cluster avoids degradation by adopting an alternative, stable, oxidized conformation.
source: Combined, our crystal structures and EPR data reveal that the metalloclusters of DvCODH are not degraded upon oxidation and that the C-cluster avoids degradation by adopting an alternative, stable, oxidized conformation.
evidence: Inference based on combined crystallographic and EPR data

claim: DvCODH regains activity upon chemical or electrochemical reduction following exposure to molecular oxygen.
source: Consistent with these results, DvCODH was recently shown to regain activity upon chemical or electrochemical reduction following exposure to molecular oxygen (Merrouch et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Merrouch et al., 2015

claim: The rearranged C-cluster scaffold can be thought of as a 'safety net' for retaining cluster ions upon oxygen exposure.
source: In this respect, the rearranged C-cluster scaffold can be thought of as a 'safety net' for retaining cluster ions upon oxygen exposure, and may explain, at least in part, the ability of certain CODHs to recover activity following oxidation in air (Merrouch et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015; Domnik et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference based on structural data and citations to Merrouch et al., 2015, Wang et al., 2015, and Domnik et al., 2017

claim: The rearranged C-cluster may explain the ability of certain CODHs to recover activity following oxidation in air.
source: In this respect, the rearranged C-cluster scaffold can be thought of as a 'safety net' for retaining cluster ions upon oxygen exposure, and may explain, at least in part, the ability of certain CODHs to recover activity following oxidation in air (Merrouch et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015; Domnik et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference based on structural data and citations

claim: The rearranged C-cluster could improve the ability of an organism to rapidly recover CODH activity after transient exposure to oxic conditions.
source: This kind of safety net could improve the ability of an organism to rapidly recover CODH activity after transient exposure to oxic conditions.
evidence: Speculation based on structural findings

claim: Cys301 is strictly conserved in CODHs but is not a ligand to the canonical C-cluster.
source: One of the more noteworthy aspects of the oxidized C-cluster is that cluster ligation involves one residue (Cys301) that is strictly conserved in CODHs but is not a ligand to the canonical C-cluster.
evidence: Direct statement based on structural analysis and sequence conservation

claim: Mutation of Cys316 (equivalent to Cys301 in DvCODH) to serine in MtCODH/ACS resulted in an inactive CODH that appeared to lack an intact C-cluster.
source: Interestingly, previous work on the heterotetrameric CODH/acetyl-CoA synthase from Moorella thermoacetica (MtCODH/ACS) showed that mutation of the equivalent cysteine residue (Cys316) to serine resulted in an inactive CODH that appeared to lack an intact C-cluster (Kim et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2004

claim: DvCODH(C301S) is inactive.
source: Similar to what was observed with MtCODH/ACS (Kim et al., 2004), DvCODH(C301S) is inactive and does not contain Ni, as assessed by CO oxidation activity assays and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES), respectively (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by CO oxidation activity assay data

claim: DvCODH(C301S) does not contain Ni.
source: Similar to what was observed with MtCODH/ACS (Kim et al., 2004), DvCODH(C301S) is inactive and does not contain Ni, as assessed by CO oxidation activity assays and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES), respectively (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by ICP-OES metal analysis data

claim: DvCODH(C301S) cannot be activated by Ni under reducing conditions.
source: Unlike wild-type DvCODH, DvCODH(C301S) cannot be activated by Ni under reducing conditions, analogous to what has been observed previously for DvCODH samples grown in the absence of the C-cluster maturation factor CooC (Hadj-Saïd et al., 2015; Merrouch et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by activity assay data and citations to Hadj-Saïd et al., 2015 and Merrouch et al., 2018

claim: The crystal structure of DvCODH(C301S) was determined to 2.0 Å resolution.
source: To investigate the architecture of a non-activatable C-cluster, we determined the crystal structure of DvCODH(C301S) to 2.0 Å resolution (Supplementary file 1)
evidence: Direct statement about crystallographic data

claim: DvCODH(C301S) has an intact [3Fe-4S] C-cluster core with an Feu ion that adopts alternative conformations.
source: To investigate the architecture of a non-activatable C-cluster, we determined the crystal structure of DvCODH(C301S) to 2.0 Å resolution (Supplementary file 1) and discovered an intact [3Fe-4S] C-cluster core with an Feu ion that adopts alternative conformations (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 5

claim: In DvCODH(C301S), approximately 70% of Feu is in its canonical position coordinated by His266 and Cys302, whereas approximately 30% is in the Ni-cubane site.
source: Approximately 70% of Feu is in its canonical position coordinated by His266 and Cys302, whereas approximately 30% is in the Ni-cubane site (see Methods; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: In the absence of the non-canonical Feu-ligand Cys301, the C-cluster cannot be activated by Ni and Feu appears to be free to occupy multiple sites.
source: Thus, in the absence of the non-canonical Feu-ligand Cys301, the cluster cannot be activated by Ni and Feu appears to be free to occupy multiple sites.
evidence: Inference based on crystallographic data of DvCODH(C301S)

claim: The novel structure of the C-cluster with Feu coordinated by Cys301 is relevant to processes beyond oxidation, specifically Ni incorporation.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the novel structure of the C-cluster that we observe here, with Feu coordinated by Cys301, is relevant to processes beyond oxidation, specifically Ni incorporation.
evidence: Inference based on mutagenesis and structural data

claim: The dramatic rearrangement observed for the C-cluster adds to a growing appreciation that the ions of great clusters are in fact mobile.
source: Regardless of its role(s), the dramatic rearrangement observed for the C-cluster adds to a growing appreciation that the ions of great clusters are in fact mobile.
evidence: Inference based on structural data and comparison to other metalloclusters

claim: The oxidized P-cluster of nitrogenase adopts an open conformation relative to its reduced form through the outward movement of two Fe ions by 1.4 and 0.9 Å with accompanying loss of S coordination.
source: The oxidized P-cluster of nitrogenase adopts an open conformation relative to its reduced form through the outward movement of two Fe ions by 1.4 and 0.9 Å with accompanying loss of S coordination in a rearrangement that is proposed to couple proton transfer to electron transfer (Figure 6a) (Peters et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peters et al., 1997 and shown in Figure 6a

claim: The P-cluster rearrangement is proposed to couple proton transfer to electron transfer.
source: The oxidized P-cluster of nitrogenase adopts an open conformation relative to its reduced form through the outward movement of two Fe ions by 1.4 and 0.9 Å with accompanying loss of S coordination in a rearrangement that is proposed to couple proton transfer to electron transfer (Figure 6a) (Peters et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peters et al., 1997

claim: Both the inhibitor CO and an artificially-incorporated Se atom are able to displace a S atom of the FeMo-cofactor.
source: More recently, Rees and coworkers demonstrated that both the inhibitor CO and an artificially-incorporated Se atom are able to displace a S atom of the cluster and furthermore that, under turnover conditions, the Se atom migrates around the cluster, sampling S positions (Figure 6b) (Spatzal et al., 2014; Spatzal et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Spatzal et al., 2014 and Spatzal et al., 2015, and shown in Figure 6b

claim: Under turnover conditions, the Se atom migrates around the FeMo-cofactor, sampling S positions.
source: More recently, Rees and coworkers demonstrated that both the inhibitor CO and an artificially-incorporated Se atom are able to displace a S atom of the cluster and furthermore that, under turnover conditions, the Se atom migrates around the cluster, sampling S positions (Figure 6b) (Spatzal et al., 2014; Spatzal et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Spatzal et al., 2014 and Spatzal et al., 2015, and shown in Figure 6b

claim: A S atom of the VFe-cofactor is displaced by a NH ligand, suggesting that cluster dynamics are likely key in catalysis.
source: Very recently, it was also revealed that the same S atom of the VFe-cofactor (containing V in place of Mo) is displaced by a NH ligand, suggesting that cluster dynamics are likely key in catalysis (Sippel et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sippel et al., 2018

claim: An O2-tolerant membrane-bound hydrogenase has a novel [4Fe-3S] cluster that undergoes redox-dependent structural changes as part of an O2-tolerance mechanism.
source: Additionally, an O2-tolerant membrane-bound hydrogenase was shown to have a novel [4Fe-3S] cluster that undergoes redox-dependent structural changes as part of an O2-tolerance mechanism (Fritsch et al., 2011; Shomura et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Fritsch et al., 2011 and Shomura et al., 2011

claim: In the [4Fe-3S] cluster of O2-tolerant membrane-bound hydrogenase, one Fe ion moves ~1.6 Å upon cluster oxidation and becomes coordinated by a protein backbone amide group.
source: one Fe ion moves ~1.6 Å upon cluster oxidation and becomes coordinated by a protein backbone amide group (Figure 6c) (Shomura et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shomura et al., 2011 and shown in Figure 6c

claim: In the C-cluster, Ni moves ~3 Å and adopts an entirely new coordination environment.
source: In the present work, the metal migration of C-cluster atoms is more dramatic than in these other examples, with Ni moving ~3 Å and adopting an entirely new coordination environment, and Feu and SL moving ~1.9 and 2.6 Å, respectively, with Feu also taking on a new coordination environment.
evidence: Direct measurement from crystallographic data

claim: In the C-cluster, Feu and SL move ~1.9 and 2.6 Å, respectively, with Feu also taking on a new coordination environment.
source: In the present work, the metal migration of C-cluster atoms is more dramatic than in these other examples, with Ni moving ~3 Å and adopting an entirely new coordination environment, and Feu and SL moving ~1.9 and 2.6 Å, respectively, with Feu also taking on a new coordination environment.
evidence: Direct measurement from crystallographic data

claim: The C-cluster rearrangement from oxidized to reduced appears to involve a 'molecular cartwheel' with Ni, Feu, and SL following the same trajectory to end up in their canonical positions.
source: This C-cluster rearrangement from oxidized to reduced appears to involve what amounts to a 'molecular cartwheel' with Ni, Feu, and SL following the same trajectory to end up in their canonical positions (Figure 4d, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: Inference based on crystallographic data shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—video 1

claim: Great clusters should not be thought of as rigid scaffolds, but rather as labile assemblies of metal with sulfide.
source: In summary, X-ray crystallography has provided views of the 'great clusters' of biology, allowing us to marvel at these incredible metallic frameworks that capture and make use of CO, H2, and N2 gases. We are increasingly finding that these frameworks should not be thought of as rigid scaffolds, but rather as labile assemblies of metal with sulfide.
evidence: Inference based on structural data from multiple metalloclusters

claim: The roles of metallocluster lability appear to be diverse, including catalysis, electron transfer, protection from oxygen damage, and possibly cluster assembly.
source: The full nature and significance of this metallocluster lability is just now beginning to emerge and the roles appear to be diverse, including catalysis, electron transfer, protection from oxygen damage, and possibly cluster assembly.
evidence: Inference based on structural and functional data

claim: DvCODH was expressed in the presence of the C-cluster maturation factor CooC.
source: DvCODH was expressed in the presence of the C-cluster maturation factor CooC, as described previously (Hadj-Saïd et al., 2015).
evidence: Direct statement about experimental methods

claim: The D. vulgaris genes encoding CODH (cooS) and the CooC maturase (cooC) were cloned into modified pBGF4 shuttle vectors under the control of the promoter of the Desulfovibrio fructosovorans Ni-Fe hydrogenase operon.
source: Briefly, the D. vulgaris genes encoding CODH (cooS) and the CooC maturase (cooC) were cloned into modified pBGF4 shuttle vectors under the control of the promoter of the Desulfovibrio fructosovorans Ni-Fe hydrogenase operon.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental methods

claim: The CODH construct was N-terminally strep-tagged.
source: The CODH construct was N-terminally strep-tagged.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental methods

claim: Protein was expressed in D. fructosovorans str. MR400.
source: Protein was expressed in D. fructosovorans str. MR400 (Rousset et al., 1991) and purified under anaerobic conditions in a Jacomex anaerobic chamber (100% N2 atmosphere) by affinity chromatography on Strep-Tactin Superflow resin, as described previously (Hadj-Saïd et al., 2015).
evidence: Direct statement about experimental methods

claim: Protein was purified under anaerobic conditions by affinity chromatography on Strep-Tactin Superflow resin.
source: Protein was expressed in D. fructosovorans str. MR400 (Rousset et al., 1991) and purified under anaerobic conditions in a Jacomex anaerobic chamber (100% N2 atmosphere) by affinity chromatography on Strep-Tactin Superflow resin, as described previously (Hadj-Saïd et al., 2015).
evidence: Direct statement about experimental methods

claim: All crystals were grown using as-isolated protein samples that were not activated with NiCl2 and sodium dithionite prior to crystallization.
source: All crystals were grown using as-isolated protein samples (i.e., samples were not activated with NiCl2 and sodium dithionite prior to crystallization).
evidence: Direct statement about experimental methods

claim: Crystals were grown anaerobically in an N2 atmosphere at 21 °C by hanging drop vapor diffusion in an MBraun anaerobic chamber.
source: Crystals were grown anaerobically in an N2 atmosphere at 21 °C by hanging drop vapor diffusion in an MBraun anaerobic chamber.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental methods

claim: All data were collected at the Advanced Photon Source (Argonne, IL) at beamline 24-ID-C at a temperature of 100 K using a Pilatus 6M pixel detector.
source: All data were collected at the Advanced Photon Source (Argonne, IL) at beamline 24-ID-C at a temperature of 100 K using a Pilatus 6M pixel detector.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental methods

claim: The initial structure of DvCODH was determined to 2.50 Å resolution by molecular replacement using data from crystals belonging to space group P212121.
source: The initial structure of DvCODH was determined to 2.50 Å resolution by molecular replacement (MR) in the program Phaser (McCoy et al., 2007) using data from crystals belonging to space group P212121.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental methods

claim: The search model for molecular replacement was generated from the structure of the CODH from Rhodospirillum rubrum (47% sequence identity; PDB ID: 1JQK).
source: The search model for MR was generated from the structure of the CODH from Rhodospirillum rubrum (47% sequence identity; PDB ID: 1JQK) by modification in Sculptor (Bunkóczi and Read, 2011) using the Schwarzenbacher algorithm (Schwarzenbacher et al., 2004) with a pruning level of 2 to truncate non-identical residues at the Cβ position.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental methods

claim: EPR samples were prepared using 57Fe-enriched DvCODH containing 13.3 57Fe/monomer and 0.5 Ni/monomer.
source: EPR samples were prepared using 57Fe-enriched DvCODH containing 13.3 57Fe/monomer and 0.5 Ni/monomer, as quantified by ICP-OES.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental methods and ICP-OES data

claim: Quantitation of the S = 1/2 [Fe-S] centers amounted to 3.2 spins/dimer.
source: Quantitation of the S = 1/2 [Fe-S] centers amounted to 3.2 spins/dimer, similar to our previous report on DvCODH (Hadj-Saïd et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by EPR spin quantification data

claim: Cred1 was 0.43 spins/dimer and Cred2 was 0.35 spins/dimer.
source: Quantification of the Cred1 and Cred2 states was carried out on the basis of numerical double-integration of the simulated spectra using the MATLAB-based EasySpin software (Stoll and Schweiger, 2006); Cred1 was 0.43 spins/dimer and Cred2 was 0.35 spins/dimer.
evidence: Supported by EPR spin quantification data

claim: This work provides the first view of an oxidized state of the C-cluster.
source: Using X-ray crystallography, we have observed unprecedented conformational dynamics in the C-cluster of the CODH from Desulfovibrio vulgaris, providing the first view of an oxidized state of the cluster.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract

claim: The novel, oxidized cluster arrangement plays a role in avoiding irreversible oxidative degradation at the C-cluster.
source: Combined with supporting spectroscopic data, our structures reveal that this novel, oxidized cluster arrangement plays a role in avoiding irreversible oxidative degradation at the C-cluster.
evidence: Inference based on combined crystallographic and spectroscopic data

claim: The oxidized conformation could be important for proper cluster assembly, in particular Ni incorporation.
source: Furthermore, mutagenesis of a conserved cysteine residue that binds the C-cluster in the oxidized state but not in the reduced state suggests that the oxidized conformation could be important for proper cluster assembly, in particular Ni incorporation.
evidence: Inference based on mutagenesis data
